newsitem.title: CONGO: Push for peace in Congo Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Push for peace in Congo Brazzaville.

text.p: The United States and France joined talks on Saturday to end a bloody showdown between Congo's President Pascal Lissouba and former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.

Despite sporadic explosions and shooting in the centre of the former French colony's capital, a truce showed signs of taking hold and France prepared to start withdrawing its soldiers after evacuating almost 5,000 foreign nationals.

A spokesman for Brazzaville mayor and mediator Bernard Kolelas said the U.S. and French ambassadors attended all-party talks to try to bring the two main players together for peace talks in neighbour and fellow oil-producer Gabon.

"If the work finishes today then they (Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso) could leave today. It's probable that they will go to Libreville in person," Hellot Mampouya told Reuters before the talks began at the French ambassador's residence.
Elite French Foreign Legion paratroopers guarded the talks.
The conflict erupted on June 5 after the army surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised arms in the runup to a July 27 election.
U.S. ambassador Aubrey Hooks said before the meeting a lull in ethnic and political fighting since Friday was encouraging.

"The two sides are talking about concrete steps and that's encouraging," he told Reuters. "I think people want elections. There may be some who do not want elections but it's the average people who want peace and a return to a day-to-day routine."

Kolelas was runner-up to Lissouba in a 1992 presidential election. His supporters were in the thick of fighting which killed at least 2,000 people in 1993 after disputed parliamentary elections. This time they have stayed clear.
He and Lissouba and Sassou Nguesso, both of whom told their forces to cease fire on Wednesday, have all said that they want the presidential election to go ahead.
Hooks, Kolelas, representatives of the two rivals and French ambassador Raymond Cesaire were preparing the ground for peace talks to be hosted by Gabon's veteran President Omar Bongo.
Kolelas and his mediation committee earlier agreed a peace blueprint envisaging measures such as assembly of fighters and joint patrols to return the battered city to normal.
Brazzaville enjoyed a relatively calm night after about an hour of sustained shooting around Brazzaville international airport after nightfall. There were reports of shooting in town.
"If you compare what has been happening yesterday and in the night with the last few days then you will definitely say the ceasefire is being respected," Kolelas spokesman Mampouya said.
Diplomats said that the U.S. and French ambassadors began contacts with the various sides two days ago.

Bodies still littered Brazzaville's streets on Friday. Aid workers and military officials had not been able to reach all areas to compile a reliable death toll, which some sources say could run into hundreds and maybe even several thousand.
France said in Paris that it would start pulling its troops out of Brazzaville on Sunday. The government did not say how long the withdrawal would take.
Sassou Nguesso, named president in 1979, bowed to pressure for multi-party politics in 1990 but was among candidates knocked out in the first round of the 1992 poll.
He returned to Congo in January after over a year in France and launched into an undeclared campaign for the presidency.
